claim: Biomimetic robots let us test mechanics and neural control
source: Asano et al. (2016); Bolen and Hunt (2019); Dissertation Ch. 1

claim: The tools make each of Hunt’s four training steps observable
source: Hunt, INRC presentation (2019), slide 44 · Dissertation Ch. 6
evidence_and_scope:
Hunt’s first step selects a CPG with an intrinsic period about twice the target stepping period. SNS blocks and open-loop traces expose that rhythm. Second, train afferent inputs to the CPG using expected feedback so transitions match walking timing; the tools provide afferent playback and transition traces. Third, train CPG/PF outputs to match MN peaks; compare motor-neuron activity under common inputs. Fourth, train Ia/Ib feedback to refine activation; use closed-loop simulations and pathway interventions. The four steps are Hunt’s training procedure. This dissertation’s staged tests check implementations and effects; they do not establish that every coupled model has completed all four steps.

Source: Hunt, INRC presentation (2019), slide 44 · Dissertation Ch. 6

claim: Two deleted bursts can preserve or reset the rhythm
source: Dissertation Ch. 6 and Appendix D · Current saved verification records
evidence_and_scope:
The reduced Deng-derived translated circuit is coupled to a suspended model. Stimuli lasting two baseline periods suppress two expected flexor motor bursts at each tested layer. RG-extensor +50 nA shifts both RG and motor timing by 0.211 cycle. PF-extensor +50 nA suppresses output without resetting the RG clock, and flexor-MN −500 nA also gives a non-resetting deletion. Read left RG traces and right MN activation together. Stronger-current controls matter: a one-second PF pulse shifts motor timing by 0.208 cycle while RG timing stays unchanged. A motor shift alone therefore does not prove RG resetting. This is a translated reduced-circuit test, not original-rat locomotion replication.
